body.p: Applicant has reviewed the Office action dated September 6 , 2022, and the references cited therein. Claims 1-13 and 16 are currently pending. Claim 16 is withdrawn from consideration. Claims 1-13 stand rejected. Claims 14-15 are canceled. Applicant's Amendments
Applicant has amended independent claim 1 to clarify the nature of the claimed first and second signals provided by respective electrodes. In particular, Applicant's claim 1 now recites:
said first electrodes being configured to cooperatively receive a first electrical
signal indicative of a membrane potential of a thoracic diaphragm of the body and for

p.u: the first electrical signal as a measurement signal;

body.p: ... the at least one second electrode thereby being arranged for receiving a second
electrical signal indicative of one or more further electric physiologic signals from the
body and for providing the second electrical signal separate from the first electrical
signal, the second electrode thereby providing a filter signal, for enabling filtering of the first electrical signal using the second electrical signal for enabling electromyography of
the thoracic diaphragm. (Emphasis added).
Support for the above clarifying claim text is provided in Applicant's original application at, for example, page 12, lines 6-21.
Applicant requests favorable reconsideration of the grounds for rejection of the

previously pending claims in view of Applicant's further amendments to the claims and remarks addressing the shortcomings of the prior art with regard to particular recited elements of the claimed invention.
Please charge any fee deficiencies to Deposit Account No. 12-1216. Grounds for Rejecting the Claims
1. Claims 1-5 and 11 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. §103 as being obvious over Connor, U.S. Pub. No. 2018/0307314 (Connor) in view of Hoskuldsson, U.S. Pub. No. 2018/0049678 (Hoskuldsson).
2. Claim 6 is rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as being unpatentable over Connor and Hoskuldsson and in view of McGrane, U.S. Pub. No. 2017/0019988 (McGrane).
3. Claim 7 is rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as being unpatentable over Connor and Hoskuldsson and in view of Maesani, U.S. Pub. No. 2017/0273590 (Maesani).

4. Claims 8 and 10 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. §103 as being unpatentable over Connor and Hoskuldsson in view of Maesani as applied to claim 7 and in further view of Muccio, U.S. Pub. No. 2012/0016440 (Muccio).
5. Claim 9 is rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as being unpatentable over Connor and Hoskuldsson and in view of Hsiao, U.S. Pub. No. 2012/0265025 (Hsiao).
6. Claim 12 is rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as being unpatentable over Connor and Hoskuldsson as applied to claim 1, and further in view of Sims, U.S. Pub. No. 2007/0293781 (Sims).
7. Claim 13 is rejected under 35 U.S.C. §103 as being unpatentable over Connor and Hoskuldsson as applied to claim 1, and further in view of Tupin, U.S. Pub. No. 2011/0060215 (Tupin).

Applicant, in view of at least the current further amendments to claim 1, traverses the grounds for each and every rejection for at least the reasons set forth herein below. Applicant addresses the specific rejections in the order they arise in the Office Action.
Applicant's Specific Responses to the Grounds for Rejection
1. Rejection of Claims 1-5 and 11 as being obvious over Connor in view of Hoskuldsson

Applicant, even without reliance upon the current clarifying amendments to independent claim 1, traverses the rejection of claims 1-5 and 11, including independent claim 1, 10, 11 and 14, as being obvious over the teachings of Connor in view of Hoskuldsson.
First, neither cited Publication has afiling date prior to Applicant's

claimed/established priority date of September 21, 2016 (the date of the Dutch priority document - which uses English text and therefor does not require a certified translation). Connor Pub. No. US 2018/0307314 was filed on June 25, 2018, and Hoskuldsson et al. Pub. No. US 2018/0049678 was filed on Aug. 18, 2017. Though both references claim priority to previously filed documents, Connor Pub. '314 is a continuation-in-part multiple (three) times to even a first application having a filing date prior to September 21, 2016; and Hoskuldsson Pub. '678 is a non-provisional application of a provisional application filed on August 19, 2016. The Office action thus improperly refers to portions of Connor and Hoskuldsson for which priority is not established in the current Office action. In the event that the current rejection is not withdrawn, Applicant specifically requests citation to the teachings of prior
art documents (i.e. a Connor application filed by September 21, 2016 and the Hoskuldsson provisional application).
Second, Applicant's claimed invention - at least in view of the current clarifications

- is not rendered obvious by the combined teachings of the cited "non-prior art" Connor and Hoskuldsson references. In that regard, a prima facie case of obviousness cannot be established with regard to currently amended independent claim 1 since the combined teachings of the cited Connor and Hoskuldsson references do not describe each recited element of any currently pending independent claim. These shortcomings are discussed in detail herein below.
Moreover, a proper reason cannot be established for one skilled in the art to modify

Connor's teachings, in view of Hoskuldsson, in a way that would result in Applicant's claimed invention. Notably, neither reference demonstrates any awareness of a particularized problem that would provide a reason to modify Connor, in view of Hoskuldsson, in a way that resulted in Applicant's claimed invention.
a. Applicant's Claimed Invention
Applicant's claimed invention is directed to a wearable device including a particular

electrode arrangement that facilitates monitoring vital signs (i.e., carrying out electromyography of the thoracic diaphragm) of its wearer. In particular claim 1, provided in clean form below, recites:
A wearable device for monitoring one or more vital signs of a human
body, the wearable device comprising:
a carrier configured to fit, while in use, fully around the human body, at an
abdominal part thereof; and
an electrode arrangement comprising a plurality of conductive electrodes,
wherein the electrodes are arranged on the carrier to be brought in contact with a

skin of the body in use, and wherein the plurality of conductive electrodes are configured for operating simultaneously to receive electric physiologic signals from the body for enabling monitoring of a membrane potential of one or more
muscles in the body,
wherein the plurality of conductive electrodes arranged on the carrier
comprise one or more first electrodes arranged on the carrier to be in contact with a side part of a torso of the body near the thoracic diaphragm, said first electrodes
being configured to cooperatively receive a first electrical signal indicative of a
membrane potential of a thoracic diaphragm of the body and for providing the

p.u: first electrical signal as a measurement signal;

body.p: wherein the plurality of conductive electrodes arranged on the carrier
further comprises at least one second electrode in addition to the one or more first electrodes, the at least one second electrode being arranged on the carrier to be in
contact with a mid front part of the abdominal part of the body simultaneously
with the first electrodes that receive the first electric signal indicative of said

membrane potential of the thoracic diaphragm of the body, wherein the carrier comprises a belt, and wherein the at least one second electrode and the one or more first electrodes are arranged on the belt, such that the at least one second
electrode is aligned with the one or more first electrodes, the at least one second
electrode thereby being arranged for receiving a second electrical signal indicative
of one or more further electric physiologic signals from the body and for

p.u: providing the second electrical signal separate from the first electrical signal, the

body.p: second electrode thereby providing a filter signal, for enabling filtering of the first
electrical signal using the second electrical signal for enabling electromyography
of the thoracic diaphragm.

Thus, Applicant's claimed invention provides a particular arrangement, including first electrodes and second electrodes that provide specifically defined first (measurement) and second (filtering) electrical signals, for monitoring activity of the thoracic diaphragm. Applicant's currently clarified claimed invention defines a configuration of the first/second electrodes on a belt (and electrical signals provided therefrom), and the first and second electrodes are aligned (on the belt) for particularly monitoring activity of the thoracic diaphragm of a wearer (e.g. the diaphragm of an infant). In that regard, the claimed invention recites placing the electrodes at aligned positions on a belt to be placed on a wearer to specifically enable acquiring signals indicating the activity of the thoracic diaphragm, which are relatively weaker (and thus more difficult to sense) than a cardiac signal. See Applicant's specification at page 3, lines 13-14. Furthermore, as shown in Applicant's FIG. 2a (included below), the thoracic diaphragm (element 16) of a baby has a curved shape. Applicant's claimed second electrode provides an additional signal that is taken from the mid front part of the body. The signal provided by the second electrode includes distortions as well as the relatively/comparatively strong cardiac signal, but does not include the thoracic diaphragm signal that, due to the curved shape of the baby's diaphragm and the (claimed) aligned arrangement of the first and second electrodes along the belt, is much weaker or absent in the area where the second electrode's signal is acquired. See Applicant's specification at page 4, lines 3-19. In this regard, Applicant's FIGs. 2a, 2b and 2c are reproduced below that illustratively depict placement of the belt (and
first/second electrodes) on a pre-term baby to facilitate acquiring signals via the first and second electrodes in accordance with Applicant's claimed invention.

specification at page 12, lines 2-5. Applicant's FIGs. 2b and 2c illustratively depict positioning of the belt with respect to the baby's front side and back side. The location of electrode 20 on the mid front side (per FIG. 2b) is advantageous over the back side - in view of the presence of the spine which diminishes the filter signal. See Applicant's specification at page 12, lines 6-12. Applicant's claimed invention is directed to a combination of first and second electrodes, and placement of specific ones of these two distinct electrodes, at specifically recited areas of the wearer, that facilitates obtaining: (1) a raw signal containing the thoracic diaphragm signal (as well as other non-thoracic diaphragm signals), and (2) a signal that facilitates filtering non- diaphragm signals to from the raw signal to obtain the thoracic diaphragm signal.
b. The Combined teachings of the cited references do not render the claimed invention

Applicant, at least in view of the current clarifying amendments to indepeent claim 1, traverses the rejection of independent claim 1 that recite substantially the same combination of elements. As noted previously above, Applicant's further clarified claimed invention is directed to a particular arrangement, including first electrodes and second electrodes that provide
specifically defined first (measurement) and second (filtering) electrical signals, for monitoring activity of the thoracic diaphragm.

The Office action relies primarily upon the teachings of Connor that, in addition to not being prior art, does not describe Applicant's first electrode providing a first (measurement) signal and a second electrode that provides a second/distinct signal that fulfills a different function from the first signal provided by the first electrode. See Connor, paragraphs [0065] and [0066]. This difference, missing from the admittedly missing teaching in Connor, is what renders Applicant's claimed invention suitable for providing an accurate signal of the relatively weak membrane potential of the thoracic diaphragm.
Connor, for example in figure 3, discloses a brace comprising electrodes 309. The

electrodes are configured for receiving electric physiologic signals muscles in the body. Also, in the configuration illustrated in figure 3 and the written description in paragraph [0075], the brace may be provided in the form of an abdominal brace, where some of the electrodes 309 may in use be located near a side part of a torso of the body. However, the brace of Connor is not designed for performing electromyography of specifically the thoracic diaphragm. Connor

does not discriminate between different signals from different electrodes 309. Thus, while Connor apparently discloses all of the electrodes 309 to obtain electromyographic signals, there is no disclosure in Connor of the electrodes "cooperatively receiving" these signals.

Importantly, even if one were to equate the receipt of signals via multiple electrodes with the cooperative receipt of a certain signal via multiple electrodes, Connor still does not describe generation/receipt of a separate second signal generated by a second electrode to provide a filter signal for the first (measurement) signal.
The Office action relies upon the teachings of Hoskuldsson to fill admitted gaps in

Connor summarized above. However, instead of filling the aforementioned gaps, Hoskuldsson describes an entirely different type of signal acquired in an entirely different way. In particular, Hoskuldsson, at paragraph [0036], describes measuring changes in the cross sectional area of the abdomen due to breathing (i.e. expansion/contraction of the abdomen). Hoskuldsson does not describe measuring/determining a membrane potential of the thoracic diaphragm. Not only is this a different type of measurement, it also a sensor intended for a much larger user, and there is no indication that such sensor is even suitable for monitoring the vital signs of a preterm baby. It
necessarily follows that Hoskuldsson does not describe using this "second" signal as a filter for the first signal in accordance with Applicant's clarified/claimed invention.
For at least the above-provided reasons, Applicant's claimed invention is not rendered obvious by the combined teachings of the cited Connor and Hoskuldsson references.
